body.text: The Newfoundland and Labrador R&D tax credit is a 15% fully refundable provincial credit on eligible SR&ED expenditures incurred in the province, claimed by corporations on Schedule T2SCH301 and by individuals on Form T1129. It has no expenditure limit, uses the federal qualified expenditure base and, as government assistance, reduces federal SR&ED qualified expenditures.

This report delivers a comprehensive technical audit and statutory analysis of the research and development (R&D) tax incentive architecture, direct innovation funding programmes, administrative compliance procedures, and governing jurisprudence in Canada as of November 2026.

Canada's foundational mechanism for incentivising private-sector R&D is the federal Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program, jointly overseen by the Department of Finance Canada (which formulates legislative tax policy) and the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA, which administers technical and financial compliance) under Section 37 and Section 127 of the federal Income Tax Act (ITA), R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), and Part XXIX (Section 2900 and Section 2902) of the Income Tax Regulations (ITR), C.R.C., c. 945. Between December 2024 and November 2026, the federal SR&ED regime underwent its most substantial legislative transformation in more than a decade. Initiated by the December 16, 2024 Fall Economic Statement (FES), expanded in the November 4, 2025 Federal Budget, enacted into law upon the Royal Assent of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, and further broadened in the November 2026 Federal Budget (Masters of our Destiny), these reforms doubled the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% refundable Investment Tax Credit (ITC) from $3.0 million to $6.0 million, raised the phase-out thresholds from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, extended the 35% enhanced refundable credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), restored the eligibility of capital expenditures and Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) acquired after December 15, 2024, launched a formal CRA Pre-Claim Approval process on April 1, 2026, and proposed expanding eligible SR&ED costs to include commercialisation and intellectual property (IP) protection expenses.
1. Statutory Architecture and 2024–2026 Legislative Reforms
1.1 Dual-Mechanism Statutory Design under the Income Tax Act

The federal SR&ED Tax Incentive Program operates through a two-pronged statutory mechanism under the Income Tax Act that separates the deduction of R&D expenditures from the calculation and application of investment tax credits. Under the first prong, Subsection 37(1) of the ITA establishes the Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures. Taxpayers carrying on a business in Canada in a taxation year may accumulate allowable current expenditures—and, for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024, allowable capital expenditures—incurred for SR&ED carried on in Canada that is related to a business of the taxpayer (or related to a business actively carried on by a related corporation under subsection 37(1.1)). The subsection 37(1) pool functions as an accumulating running balance recalculated each year. Rather than capitalising and depreciating R&D expenses over multi-year Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) schedules, a corporate or individual claimant may deduct the entire available pool balance in the current taxation year to reduce net business income, deduct only a partial amount, or carry forward any undeducted positive balance indefinitely to offset business income in future taxation years. By contrast, under paragraph 96(1)(e.1) of the ITA, a partnership must deduct its entire pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures at the partnership level in the taxation year incurred and cannot carry forward any pool balance to subsequent taxation years.

Under the second prong, Subsections 127(5), 127(9), and 127.1(1) of the ITA govern the SR&ED Investment Tax Credit (ITC). In addition to deducting expenditures from business income via the subsection 37(1) pool, claimants earn an ITC calculated as a statutory percentage (either the 35% enhanced rate or the 15% basic rate) of their annual "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool" determined at the end of the taxation year under subsection 127(9). Unlike the deductible pool under subsection 37(1), the qualified expenditure pool under subsection 127(9) is calculated strictly on an annual basis and does not carry over from one taxation year to the next. Depending on the legal classification of the claimant, whether the underlying expenditure is of a current or capital nature, and whether the expenditure falls within the claimant's annual expenditure limit, earned ITCs may be applied to reduce federal Part I tax otherwise payable to nil under subsection 127(5), refunded in cash under subsection 127.1(1), carried back up to 3 preceding taxation years, or carried forward up to 20 subsequent taxation years.

To prevent duplicative tax benefits between the subsection 37(1) deduction and the section 127 tax credit, paragraph 37(1)(e) of the ITA requires that any federal SR&ED ITC deducted against Part I tax payable, carried back to a prior year, or refunded in cash in a given taxation year must be deducted from the claimant's subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures in the immediately following taxation year. Conversely, provincial and territorial R&D tax credits (unless formally renounced by the statutory deadline where permitted) and direct government grants or non-government assistance constitute assistance under subsection 127(9) and paragraph 37(1)(d), reducing both the subsection 37(1) deductible pool and the subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure pool in the current taxation year in which the expenditures are incurred. If these mandatory reductions (such as prior-year federal ITCs or current-year assistance) cause the subsection 37(1) pool balance to become negative at the end of a taxation year, paragraph 12(1)(v) of the ITA requires the negative amount to be included directly in the taxpayer's net business income for that taxation year, while paragraph 37(1)(c.1) adds an equal amount back to the pool in the following taxation year to reset the opening pool balance to nil.
1.2 Chronology of the 2024–2026 Federal SR&ED Modernisation

Auditing or preparing Canadian R&D claims across the 2024, 2025, and 2026 taxation years requires tracking four sequential legislative and administrative milestones that reshaped expenditure limits, corporate eligibility, and qualifying cost categories.

First, on December 16, 2024, the federal government tabled the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (FES) following national consultations on modernising Canada's R&D framework. For taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024 (i.e., after December 15, 2024), the 2024 FES initially proposed increasing the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% ITC from $3.0 million to $4.5 million, raising the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, extending the 35% enhanced refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) subject to a three-year average gross revenue phase-out between $15 million and $75 million, allowing Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) to elect to use the gross revenue phase-out structure instead of taxable capital, and restoring pre-2014 eligibility rules for SR&ED capital expenditures and lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024. Although the prorogation of Parliament in early 2025 delayed immediate introduction of a bill, the Department of Finance released comprehensive draft legislative proposals on August 15, 2025, codifying the 2024 FES architecture.

Second, on November 4, 2025, the Minister of Finance and National Revenue, François-Philippe Champagne, tabled Budget 2025. Budget 2025 confirmed the government's intention to enact the 2024 FES and August 2025 draft legislative measures, and introduced a major expansion: it further increased the annual expenditure limit on which the enhanced 35% refundable SR&ED ITC can be earned from the previously proposed $4.5 million to $6.0 million, effective retroactively for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. Industry analyses of Budget 2025 noted that the SR&ED enhancements were projected to cost $3 million in 2025–26, ramping up to $70 million in 2026–27 and $293 million over five years. In parallel with the SR&ED reforms, Budget 2025 proposed temporary immediate expensing (a 100% deduction in the first taxation year of use) for eligible manufacturing or processing (M&P) buildings (and eligible additions or alterations) acquired on or after Budget Day and first used before 2030, provided at least 90% of the building's floor space is used for M&P (with enhanced first-year CCA rates phasing down to 75% for property first used in 2030 or 2031, 55% in 2032 or 2033, and nil after 2033), alongside immediate expensing for productivity-enhancing assets such as patents, data network infrastructure, and computers.

Third, on March 26, 2026, Bill C-15 received Royal Assent, formally enacting the $6.0 million expenditure limit, ECPC eligibility, the $15 million–$75 million phase-out thresholds, the CCPC gross revenue election, and the restoration of capital expenditures and Shared-Use Equipment into the Income Tax Act. Less than one week later, on April 1, 2026, the CRA launched its new optional Pre-Claim Approval process within My Business Account, followed by the publication of revised Form T661 and Form T1145 on May 15, 2026, and updated CRA administrative policy documents between May and October 2026.

Fourth, on November 5, 2026, the federal government tabled Budget 2026 (Masters of our Destiny), proposing to expand the SR&ED programme to cover commercialisation expenses incurred in taxation years beginning on or after Budget Day. Specifically, Budget 2026 proposes to make expenses associated with bringing a new product or process to market—namely obtaining necessary regulatory approvals or certifications and securing and maintaining intellectual property (IP) protection—eligible for SR&ED tax incentives, delivering an estimated $930 million over five years ($235 million ongoing). Budget 2026 further specifies that if a taxpayer subsequently disposes of IP for which SR&ED support was claimed in respect of IP protection costs, recapture rules will apply to recover the related SR&ED deduction and ITC amounts, and directs the CRA to publish sector-specific guidance on commercialisation eligibility. Beyond tax credits, Budget 2026 announced $1.0 billion over six years (starting in 2028–29) for the Strategic Response Fund (formerly the Strategic Innovation Fund) to support large-scale R&D projects in AI, agri-food, bio-manufacturing, and clean tech, $45 million over five years (starting in 2027–28) to Natural Resources Canada for EV charging infrastructure R&D, and Patent Act amendments requiring mandatory registration of patent ownership changes with the Canadian Intellectual Property Office (CIPO) alongside new regulations curbing abusive patent demand letters.

body.text: 2. Federal SR&ED Tax Credit Rates, Thresholds, Refundability, and Carryover Rules
2.1 Enhanced (35%) versus Basic (15%) Investment Tax Credit Rates

The federal SR&ED programme operates a two-tiered credit structure under Section 127 of the Income Tax Act. The Enhanced SR&ED ITC Rate of 35%—which consists of the 15% basic rate plus a 20% enhancement—is available on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to the corporation's annual expenditure limit. For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, only qualifying Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) could earn this 35% rate on up to $3.0 million of annual qualified expenditures. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, both qualifying CCPCs and Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) earn the 35% enhanced rate on up to $6.0 million of annual qualified expenditures, doubling the maximum annual enhanced ITC pool from $1.05 million to $2.1 million.

The Basic (General) SR&ED ITC Rate of 15% applies to all qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred by corporations that are neither qualifying CCPCs nor ECPCs (such as foreign-controlled Canadian subsidiaries or large public corporations whose expenditure limit has been eliminated), to qualified SR&ED expenditures of CCPCs and ECPCs that exceed their available annual expenditure limit, and to unincorporated claimants including sole proprietorships (individuals), partners of a partnership, and beneficiaries of a trust. In addition, Crown corporations (other than Prescribed Federal Crown Corporations) are excluded from earning SR&ED ITCs because their income is exempt from Part I tax under the Income Tax Act.
2.2 Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs)

Enacted for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) regime eliminates the long-standing structural cliff where domestic innovation companies lost access to the 35% refundable SR&ED tax credit upon listing their shares on a public stock exchange. To qualify as an ECPC throughout a taxation year, a corporation must satisfy three cumulative statutory criteria:

items: The corporation must be resident in Canada throughout the taxation year.
The corporation must have a class of shares listed on a designated stock exchange (or have elected, or been designated by the Minister of National Revenue, to be a public corporation).

The corporation must not be controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-resident persons, and would not be controlled by a particular person if each share of the corporation owned by a non-resident person were owned by that particular person.

body.text: Furthermore, Canadian-resident subsidiary corporations that are all or substantially all (90% or more) owned by one or more ECPCs are also eligible to access the enhanced 35% refundable ITC, sharing the corporate group's $6.0 million expenditure limit.
2.3 Expenditure Limit Phase-Out Mechanics: Taxable Capital vs. Gross Revenue Election

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the $6.0 million annual expenditure limit phases out on a straight-line basis once a corporation (or its associated/consolidated group) exceeds specific size thresholds. Under the post-December 15, 2024 rules, two distinct phase-out calculation methods exist.

Under the Taxable Capital Reduction Method (Default for CCPCs), a CCPC's expenditure limit is reduced based on the taxable capital employed in Canada by the corporation (and all associated CCPCs) for the immediately preceding taxation year. For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the $3.0 million expenditure limit began to decrease at $10.0 million of prior-year taxable capital and became nil at $50.0 million (decreasing by $0.075 for every $1.00 of taxable capital above $10.0 million). For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the $6.0 million expenditure limit begins to decrease when prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada reaches $15.0 million and becomes nil when prior-year taxable capital reaches $75.0 million. Associated CCPCs must allocate the resulting expenditure limit among themselves using Schedule T2SCH49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit) pursuant to subsection 127(10.3) of the ITA.

Under the Three-Year Average Gross Revenue Reduction Method (Mandatory for ECPCs; Elective for CCPCs), ECPCs are required (under subsection 127(10.6) of the ITA)—and CCPCs may formally elect under subsection 127(10.31) (standalone CCPCs) or subsection 127(10.32) of the ITA (associated CCPCs)—to determine their expenditure limit reduction using their average annual gross revenue over the 3 preceding fiscal years rather than taxable capital. This election provides substantial relief to capital-intensive scale-ups (such as biotechnology, clean technology, or hardware manufacturers) that hold more than $15.0 million in balance-sheet equity or debt capital while generating less than $15.0 million in revenue. Under the gross revenue structure, the expenditure limit remains at the full $6.0 million when 3-year average annual gross revenue is $15.0 million or less, is reduced on a straight-line basis when 3-year average annual gross revenue is between $15.0 million and $75.0 million, and is eliminated at $75.0 million. For standalone corporations, gross revenue is the amount reported in annual GAAP financial statements presented to shareholders. For corporations that are members of a consolidated corporate group preparing consolidated financial statements, the expenditure limit is shared among group members, and the 3-year average annual revenue under subsection 127(10.6) is calculated using the consolidated financial statements at the highest level of consolidation (including the preceding 3 fiscal years' revenue of each corporation that is a member of the group in the tax year, regardless of whether the corporations were associated throughout the entire 3-year period).

Mathematically, the expenditure limit reduction formulas across the pre-December 16, 2024 and post-December 15, 2024 regimes operate as follows (noting that under the August 2025 draft legislation based on the interim $4.5 million limit across the $60 million band from $15 million to $75 million, the reduction slope was $0.075 per dollar, whereas under the enacted Budget 2025 / Bill C-15 $6.0 million limit over the same $60 million band from $15 million to $75 million, the straight-line reduction from $6.0 million to zero equals $0.10 per dollar):

items: Taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024: Expenditure limit = $3,000,000 × [($40,000,000 − A) ÷ $40,000,000], where A is the lesser of $40,000,000 and the amount by which prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $10,000,000.

Taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024: Expenditure limit = $6,000,000 × [($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000], where A is nil if the relevant amount (prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada, or 3-year average annual revenue for ECPCs and electing CCPCs) is $15,000,000 or less, and otherwise the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which that relevant amount exceeds $15,000,000.

2.4 Refundability Rates and Carryover Rules

When a claimant's SR&ED ITCs exceed its federal Part I tax otherwise payable in the taxation year, subsection 127.1(1) of the ITA governs whether the unused current-year ITC balance can be refunded in cash. Under subsection 127.1(3), any ITC refunded in cash is deemed to have been deducted against Part I tax payable in the year, thereby reducing the ITC balance available for carryback or carryforward and reducing the following year's subsection 37(1) deductible pool.

With the restoration of capital expenditure eligibility after December 15, 2024, the refundability rate depends on whether the underlying expenditure is a current expenditure (including the Prescribed Proxy Amount, which is 100% refundable at the 35% rate) or a capital expenditure (which is 40% refundable at the 35% rate). Furthermore, CRA policy distinguishes between "Qualifying CCPCs" and "Non-Qualifying CCPCs" (CCPCs whose prior-year taxable income or taxable capital exceeds the qualifying threshold for the 40% refund on basic 15% ITCs, but whose expenditure limit has not yet phased out to nil).

body.text: A specific statutory exception applies to repayments of government or non-government assistance or contract payments: while a claimant earns an ITC when it repays assistance that previously reduced qualified expenditures (computed at the historical rate that applied in the tax year the assistance was originally received), SR&ED ITC refunds cannot be claimed in respect of repayments of assistance or contract payments.

Under subsection 127(5) of the ITA, any current-year SR&ED ITC that is not applied to reduce Part I tax payable and is not refunded in cash may be carried back up to 3 preceding taxation years or carried forward up to 20 subsequent taxation years. For a carryback to any of the 3 preceding taxation years, the allowable carryback is strictly limited to the lesser of: (1) the current-year ITC to the extent that it was not deductible to reduce Part I tax otherwise payable in the current year, and (2) the amount by which Part I tax otherwise payable in the previous taxation year exceeds the ITC already available in that previous year. Consequently, a claimant cannot carry back an ITC amount that could have been used to reduce current-year Part I tax to nil. As illustrated in the CRA's SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, if a corporation has $10,000 of Part I tax and $6,000 of ITC in Year 1 ($4,000 net tax), and $12,000 of Part I tax and $15,000 of ITC in Year 2, the corporation has $3,000 of excess ITC in Year 2 above its Year 2 Part I tax ($15,000 minus $12,000) and may carry back the lesser of $3,000 or $4,000—namely $3,000—to Year 1. Both the 3-year carryback of ITCs earned after an acquisition of control and the 20-year carryforward of ITCs earned before an acquisition of control are subject to statutory streaming restrictions.
3. Qualifying Work: Statutory Definition and the "Why" and "How" Eligibility Framework
3.1 The Statutory Definition of SR&ED (Subsection 248(1) of the ITA)

For any expenditure to qualify for federal or provincial SR&ED tax incentives, the underlying technical work must meet the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. The preamble of subsection 248(1) defines SR&ED as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis" and encompasses four categories of eligible work under paragraphs (a) to (d):

items: Basic Research (Paragraph 248(1)(a)): Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view.
Applied Research (Paragraph 248(1)(b)): Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view.

Experimental Development (Paragraph 248(1)(c)): Work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Experimental development is the most common category claimed by Canadian businesses.

Support Work (Paragraph 248(1)(d)): Work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to only eight exhaustive categories—namely (1) engineering, (2) design, (3) operations research, (4) mathematical analysis, (5) computer programming, (6) data collection, (7) testing, or (8) psychological research—where the work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of basic research, applied research, or experimental development described in paragraphs (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada. Support work is never SR&ED on its own; it derives its eligibility strictly from the core paragraph (a), (b), or (c) SR&ED work it supports.

body.text: Conversely, paragraphs 248(1)(e) to (k) of the ITA explicitly exclude seven categories of commercial and routine work from the definition of SR&ED, even if carried out alongside an R&D project:

items: Paragraph (e): Market research or sales promotion.
Paragraph (f): Quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes.
Paragraph (g): Research in the social sciences or the humanities.
Paragraph (h): Prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas.
Paragraph (i): The commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product, or the commercial use of a new or improved process.
Paragraph (j): Style changes.
Paragraph (k): Routine data collection.

body.text: As the CRA's Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives explain, the decisive factor distinguishing eligible support work under paragraph (d) (such as testing or data collection) from excluded work under paragraphs (f) or (k) (routine testing or routine data collection) is purpose. When data collection or testing is carried out specifically for the purpose of directly supporting scientific research or experimental development (i.e., testing a hypothesis to resolve technological uncertainty), it qualifies under paragraph (d); when conducted for normal business operations, routine quality assurance, or mineral prospecting, it must be excluded from the claim.
3.2 Evolution from the Five Judicial Questions to the CRA's "Why" and "How" Methodology

Tracing the administrative history of SR&ED eligibility guidance, pre-1985 claims were governed by Interpretation Bulletin IT-439 until the May 23, 1985 federal budget papers and the 1986 release of Information Circular IC 86-4 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development, later revised as IC 86-4R3 in 1994) established three foundational pillars: scientific or technological advancement, scientific or technological uncertainty, and scientific and technical content. In 1998, Justice Bowman's ruling in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen (98 DTC 1839) synthesized IC 86-4R3 and the statutory text into five criteria, which the CRA codified as the "five questions" in its Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy (published in 2012, revised in 2015, and archived in August 2021):

items: Was there a scientific or a technological uncertainty?
Did the effort involve formulating hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that uncertainty?
Was the overall approach adopted consistent with a systematic investigation or search, including formulating and testing the hypotheses by means of experiment or analysis?
Was the overall approach undertaken for the purpose of achieving a scientific or a technological advancement?
Was a record of the hypotheses tested and the results kept as the work progressed?

body.text: On August 13, 2021, the CRA replaced the archived 2015 policy with the Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives, consolidating the five questions into two overarching statutory requirements—the "Why" Requirement and the "How" Requirement—while confirming that both the five questions and the two requirements derive from the unchanged definition in subsection 248(1) of the ITA.

The "Why" Requirement governs the scientific or technological purpose of the investigation. Work must be conducted to advance scientific knowledge or achieve a technological advancement by generating or discovering conceptual knowledge (such as new theories, principles, or predictive models) rather than merely collecting factual measurements. New knowledge is required only when a scientific or technological uncertainty exists—meaning it is unknown whether a given result or objective can be achieved due to an insufficiency in the available scientific or technological knowledge base (which encompasses both internal corporate resources and publicly accessible knowledge available to competent professionals in the field). Indicators of insufficient technological knowledge include situations where existing design methods are inapplicable, specifications conflict with existing standards, parameters fall outside normal operating ranges, too many unknown variables interact, or interlocking constraints prevent a standard solution (including where meeting reasonable cost targets introduces genuine technological constraints, although cost targets alone do not create technological uncertainty). Acquiring existing knowledge or know-how through employee training, on-the-job learning, hiring expert consultants, purchasing proprietary technology, or circumventing an uncertainty via a known workaround does not satisfy the "Why" requirement. Conversely, if the purpose of the work was genuinely to resolve technological uncertainty and achieve technological advancement, whether the project ultimately succeeds or fails does not affect its eligibility.

The "How" Requirement governs the methodology of the investigation: the work must be a systematic investigation or search carried out by means of experiment or analysis. Following standard business or engineering procedures alone is insufficient. Instead, the claimant must execute and document four sequential steps:

items: Formulating a Hypothesis: Generating an idea consistent with known facts—expressed as a proposed solution, method, or causal relationship—that serves as a starting point for further investigation to prove or disprove that idea.

Testing by Experiment or Analysis: Testing the hypothesis through structured physical experiments or mathematical/computational analysis, allowing the hypothesis to evolve and be modified as test data is gathered.
Developing Logical Conclusions: Drawing objective, logical conclusions based on the experimental or analytical results.
Keeping Contemporaneous Evidence: Maintaining records and evidence of the hypotheses tested and the results obtained as the work progresses.

body.text: 4. Qualifying Expenditures (QREs), Proxy vs. Traditional Overhead, and Restored Capital Rules
4.1 Salaries and Wages (ITA s. 37 & s. 248(1); Form T661 Lines 300–315)

Under the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy and subsection 248(1) of the ITA, "salary or wages" means income of a taxpayer from an office or employment as computed under Subdivision a of Division B of Part I of the Act (Sections 5 to 8, i.e., T4 employment remuneration). Allowable inclusions comprise base salaries and wages incurred on or in respect of SR&ED, vacation pay, statutory holiday pay, sick leave pay, pay in lieu of termination notice, tips or gratuities, honorariums, director's fees, management fees, commissions, inducement and non-competition payments, cash outlays for taxable benefits under Section 6, and—exclusively for employees other than specified employees—bonuses and remuneration based on profits. Non-cash taxable benefits may be included in SR&ED salary or wages only if three conditions are met: the value is a reasonable estimate of actual employer costs, the value excludes GST/HST or PST (unless no input tax credit can be claimed), and the underlying actual costs are not claimed elsewhere as a business expense.

Conversely, the following items are strictly excluded from SR&ED salary or wages: the employer's share of related employee benefits (such as employer CPP, EI, or payroll health taxes—which cannot be included in the salary base under the Proxy Method, though under the Traditional Method the employer's share of related benefits directly linked to SR&ED employees may be claimed as overhead on line 360), extended vacation or sick leave, stock option benefits under Section 7, and retiring allowances (although under the Traditional Method, a portion of a retiring allowance may be claimed as overhead on line 360 if directly related and incremental based on the employee's historical SR&ED salary ratio and years of service, as illustrated in CRA policy where 60% of a $210,000 retiring allowance—$126,000—was allowed).

The scope of eligible employee duties depends on the overhead method elected. When a claimant elects the Proxy Method, only the salary or wages of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada may be claimed and included in the salary base. "Directly engaged" refers to hands-on technical work and direct first-line technological supervision determined by the actual tasks performed rather than the employee's job title. When a claimant uses the Traditional Method, salary or wages of employees directly undertaking, supervising, or supporting the prosecution of SR&ED are claimed directly (where direct supervision requires a significant technological background and excludes general management, though it may include long-term strategic planning or contract administration performed by a direct technological supervisor), while clerical and administrative staff salaries that pass both the "directly related" and "incremental" tests may be claimed as overhead on line 360 of Form T661.
Two timing and geographic restrictions apply to all SR&ED salary claims:

items: The 180-Day Unpaid Remuneration Rule (Section 78 of the ITA): Any accrued salary or wages that are not paid within 180 days from the end of the taxation year in which the expense was incurred are deemed not to have been incurred in that taxation year. Unpaid wages must be identified on line 315 of Form T661 in the year accrued and are deemed to be incurred—and claimed on line 310 of Form T661—in the subsequent taxation year in which they are actually paid (a payment made on the 180th day is accepted by the CRA as timely). Reasonable vacation or holiday pay and salary deferral arrangements unpaid at 180 days are deemed paid by the ITA and may be claimed as allowable wages, but are excluded from the PPA salary base.

SR&ED Work Performed Outside Canada (10% Limit under Subsection 37(1.5) of the ITA): Permissible salary or wages for SR&ED work performed outside Canada (reported on line 307 for non-specified employees and line 309 for specified employees) are limited in total to a maximum of 10% of the total SR&ED salary or wages incurred for work performed inside Canada (line 306 of Form T661). Specifically, the maximum allowable amount on line 309 for specified employees outside Canada equals 10% of line 306 minus the amount claimed on line 307.

body.text: Statutory Restrictions on "Specified Employees" (ITA s. 248(1) & ITR s. 2900(7))

A "specified employee" is an employee who is a specified shareholder (owning, directly or indirectly at any time in the year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or any related corporation, including shares owned by non-arm's length persons) or who does not deal at arm's length with the employer (such as a spouse, brother, sister, or relative of a controlling shareholder). Three statutory caps govern specified employees:

items: Prohibition on Bonuses and Profit-Based Remuneration: Bonuses and remuneration based on profits paid to a specified employee are completely excluded from allowable SR&ED salary or wages.

Direct SR&ED Salary Cap (5 × YMPE): Under the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy, the maximum direct salary or wages that a claimant can claim as an SR&ED expenditure for a specified employee is limited to 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under Section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan for the calendar year in which the tax year ends, prorated for the number of days in the taxation year on which the individual is a specified employee: Maximum direct SR&ED salary or wages = 5 × YMPE × (number of days in the taxation year on which the individual is a specified employee ÷ 365).

Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Salary Base Cap (ITR Subsection 2900(7)): Under subsection 2900(7) of the Income Tax Regulations (computed on lines 850 to 858 in Part 5 of Form T661), the maximum amount that a claimant can include in the salary base for a specified employee when calculating the 55% PPA is restricted to the lesser of:

75% of the specified employee's total salary or wages for the year (combining both SR&ED and non-SR&ED duties, and excluding bonuses, remuneration based on profits, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid wages paid in the year); or

2.5 × YMPE for the calendar year in which the claimant's tax year ends, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year that the claimant employed the individual (with no proration for days the employee was not a specified employee): PPA salary base cap = 2.5 × YMPE × (number of days in the taxation year on which the claimant employed the individual ÷ 365).

body.text: 4.2 Overhead and Other Expenditures: The Proxy Method vs. Traditional Method Election

Under subsection 37(10) of the ITA and the CRA's Traditional and Proxy Methods Policy and Prescribed Proxy Amount Policy, a claimant must elect on lines 160 and 162 of Form T661 whether to claim overhead under the Proxy Method or the Traditional Method for the taxation year.

When a claimant elects the Proxy Method, it does not specifically identify, track, or include actual SR&ED overhead and other expenditures in its SR&ED claim. Instead, under subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations, the claimant computes a notional amount—the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA)—equal to 55% of the salary base (reduced from 65% in 2012 and 60% in 2013 to 55% for 2014 and all subsequent years). The salary base consists of the salaries and wages of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada, excluding taxable benefits under Section 6, stock option benefits under Section 7, unpaid amounts under Section 78, prior-year unpaid wages paid in the current year (line 310), bonuses, and remuneration based on profits (reported as exclusions on line 812 in Part 5 of Form T661), and subject to the specified employee restrictions under ITR subsection 2900(7) and an overall cap. Because the PPA is a notional calculation, neither the PPA nor the actual overhead expenditures it represents are included in the subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures; instead, the claimant deducts its actual overhead expenses as ordinary business deductions under regular income tax rules. However, the PPA forms part of the claimant's qualified SR&ED expenditures under subsection 127(9) and earns SR&ED Investment Tax Credits at the applicable 35% or 15% rate. As demonstrated in Section 6.10 of the CRA's Traditional and Proxy Methods Policy, a company with $100,000 in directly engaged salaries, $15,000 in materials, and $50,000 in actual overhead has $165,000 in qualified expenditures under the Traditional Method (earning $57,750 in ITCs at 35%), versus $115,000 in allowable pool expenditures plus a $55,000 PPA ($100,000 × 55%) = $170,000 in qualified expenditures under the Proxy Method (earning $59,500 in ITCs at 35%).

When a claimant elects the Traditional Method, no PPA is calculated. Instead, the claimant tracks and allocates actual overhead and other expenditures on line 360 of Form T661, which are included in both the subsection 37(1) deductible pool and the subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure pool. Under paragraph 2900(2)(c) and subsection 2900(3) of the Income Tax Regulations—and as interpreted by the Tax Court of Canada in Ergorecherche et Conseils Inc. v. The Queen (98 DTC 1710) and Quantetics Corporation v. The Queen (2000 DTC 2177)—each overhead expenditure (or allocated portion thereof) must pass two mandatory tests:

items: The "Directly Related" Test: The expenditure must connect directly, without an intervening step or intermediary, to the SR&ED work, the SR&ED staff, or the machinery and equipment used by staff to perform SR&ED in Canada.

The "Incremental" Test: The expenditure must be one that would not have been incurred had the prosecution of SR&ED not occurred. Fixed monthly costs for telephones, cellular plans, or base internet service fail the incremental test and are disallowed, whereas specific identifiable charges such as incremental long-distance calls or dedicated R&D cloud/software environments qualify. Similarly, under Section 4.5 of the CRA's SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy, headhunter fees, recruiting advertisements, interview travel costs, and immigration/work-permit fees are disallowed as regular business expenses, whereas moving expenses to relocate selected candidates or SR&ED employees to another Canadian facility, taxable housing-loss benefits (ITA subsections 6(19)–(20)), and SR&ED employee training costs qualify under the Traditional Method if directly related and incremental.

body.text: 4.3 Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed and the 20-Year ITC Recapture Rule

Under the CRA's Materials for SR&ED Policy (updated March 27, 2026), "materials for SR&ED" are defined as physical and tangible raw materials, substances, or component items (in a solid, liquid, or gaseous state) that compose the body of a tangible object at a given moment in the SR&ED process—either the object on which SR&ED is performed or the object resulting from the SR&ED. Material costs can only be claimed in the taxation year in which the materials are actually consumed (line 320 of Form T661) or transformed (line 325 of Form T661) in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada under subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I)–(II), subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V), and ITR paragraph 2900(2)(a), not when purchased into inventory. Items such as laboratory glassware (test tubes, pipettes, vials, beakers, flasks, petri dishes), cleaning supplies, computer discs/CDs/DVDs, engine lubricants, and general utilities (water, electricity, natural gas, unless energy or water is directly integral to a chemical or physical material conversion process) are not materials for SR&ED; they are overhead items claimable only under the Traditional Method.

The distinction between materials consumed and materials transformed carries critical audit consequences under the Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit rules in subsections 127(27) to 127(36) of the ITA and the CRA's Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy. Materials consumed are destroyed, absorbed, or rendered virtually valueless during testing and are never subject to ITC recapture. By contrast, materials transformed (as well as ASA capital equipment and Shared-Use Equipment) are incorporated into a prototype, custom product, experimental production run (ED+EP), commercial production run with experimental development (ED+CP), or commercial asset that retains economic value.

Under subsection 127(27) and subsection 127(36) of the ITA, ITC recapture is triggered if four conditions are met: (1) the claimant acquired a property from a person or partnership in the current taxation year or in any of the 20 preceding taxation years (extended from 10 years to 20 years by subsection 127(36)); (2) the cost of the property was a qualified SR&ED expenditure; (3) a percentage of the property's cost was included in computing the claimant's ITC; and (4) the claimant disposes of the property (or a product incorporating it) or converts it to commercial use within that 20-year window. When triggered, the claimant must add back to its Part I tax payable for the year of disposition or conversion an amount equal to the lesser of the original ITC earned on the property or the historical ITC rate (35% or 15%, or 20% for pre-2014 basic credits) multiplied by the proceeds of disposition (if sold to an arm's-length party) or the fair market value (FMV) of the property (if converted to commercial use or transferred to a non-arm's length party).

Crucially, under subsection 127(32) of the ITA, "cost" for recapture purposes cannot exceed the amount paid to acquire tangible property from a third party and excludes internal salaries, wages, overhead, energy used to manufacture an internal component prior to SR&ED, property not acquired from another person (such as farm-born livestock or oil produced during experimental drilling), and intellectual property. As illustrated in Section 7.1.1 of the CRA's Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, if a claimant pays an arm's-length supplier $12,000 ($10,000 manufacturing cost plus $2,000 profit) to fabricate a custom part that is later converted to commercial use, the entire $12,000 is subject to ITC recapture; if the claimant manufactures that same part in-house, there is zero recapture on the internal salaries and overhead. Any recaptured ITC added to Part I tax payable (calculated on Schedule T2SCH31 or Form T2038(IND)) may be offset by unused ITC carryforwards and is added back to the claimant's subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures in the following taxation year under paragraph 37(1)(c.2).
4.4 Subcontractors, Non-Arm's Length Transactions, Third-Party Payments, and Prescribed Exclusions

Under the CRA's Contract Expenditures for SR&ED Performed on Behalf of a Claimant Policy and Total Qualified SR&ED Expenditures for Investment Tax Credit Purposes Policy, when a claimant contracts an arm's-length taxable supplier (a Canadian resident or a non-resident operating through a Canadian permanent establishment) to perform SR&ED in Canada on its behalf (reported on line 340 of Form T661), 100% of the expenditure is included in the subsection 37(1) deductible pool, but only 80% qualifies for SR&ED ITCs under subsection 127(9) (the 20% reduction is subtracted on line 529 of Form T661). Payments to non-taxable foreign suppliers are excluded from ITCs on line 528. If an arm's-length SR&ED contract expenditure remains unpaid 180 days after the end of the taxation year, 100% of the unpaid expenditure is excluded in that year (line 520), and 80% is added to qualified expenditures in the subsequent year when paid.

Where a claimant enters into an SR&ED contract with a non-arm's length (NAL) performer (such as a parent, subsidiary, or sister corporation under Section 251 of the ITA), the payer's expenditure is deductible in its subsection 37(1) pool under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01), but is excluded from earning ITCs under paragraph (f) of the definition of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9). Instead, the NAL performer claims its own qualified expenditures (and the payment from the NAL payer is not deemed a "contract payment" that reduces the performer's claim). However, under subsection 127(13) of the ITA, the NAL performer (transferor) and NAL payer (transferee) may file Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) to transfer qualified expenditures from the performer (deducted on line 546 of the performer's T661) to the payer (added on line 510 of the payer's T661). The transferable amount is capped at the least of three amounts:

items: The agreed amount specified by the parties on Form T1146;
The performer's SR&ED qualified expenditure pool at the end of its tax year before deducting the transfer (including the performer's PPA, if applicable); and

The total amount that would constitute an arm's-length contract payment for the SR&ED performed, provided the payer pays the performer—and the performer pays its underlying expenditures—on or before 180 days after the end of the performer's taxation year.

body.text: If a performer attempts to transfer an amount exceeding its qualified expenditure pool, the Income Tax Act voids the entire transfer so that no amount can be transferred, and partnerships cannot transfer or receive expenditures via Form T1146 because a partnership is not a "person" for purposes of subsection 127(13). Additionally, when a claimant purchases tangible goods or non-SR&ED services (including post-December 15, 2024 equipment leases, which are deemed services valued at normal accounting depreciation) from a NAL supplier, subsection 127(11.6) restricts the qualified expenditure to the lesser of the actual price incurred or the supplier's adjusted selling cost / adjusted service cost (with adjustments reported on lines 542 and 543 of Form T661, and with gifts acquired by a NAL supplier carrying an adjusted cost of nil).

Under the CRA's Third-Party Payments Policy, a claimant may also claim 80% (for ITC purposes, 100% for subsection 37(1) deduction purposes) of Third-Party Payments (reported on line 370 of Form T661 and detailed on Form T1263, Third-Party Payments for SR&ED) made in cash or in kind (at fair market value) to approved universities, colleges, research institutes, granting councils, non-profit SR&ED corporations, or other Canadian-resident corporations (including via agricultural check-off dues). Unlike an SR&ED contract (where the payer controls the work, holds exclusive IP rights, and accounts on an accrual basis), a third-party payment involves research controlled by the performing institution (usually basic or applied research with multiple funders), is accounted for on a cash basis, and requires that the SR&ED carried on in Canada relate to a business of the claimant and that the claimant be entitled to exploit the results.

Finally, under Section 2902 of the Income Tax Regulations, prescribed expenditures are strictly excluded from qualified SR&ED expenditures (reported on lines 530 and 532 of Form T661). Prescribed expenditures include general administration or management salaries and benefits (unless directly attributable under the Regulations), legal or accounting fees, interest and financing costs, entertainment expenses, advertising or selling expenses, conference or convention expenses, scientific or technical society membership dues, fines or penalties, fees paid to consultants or accountants for preparing the SR&ED claim itself, and acquisitions of used depreciable capital property.
4.5 Restored Capital Expenditures, Lease Costs, and Shared-Use Equipment (Post-December 15, 2024)

Following the enactment of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, the eligibility of SR&ED capital expenditures and equipment lease costs was restored for property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024, and lease amounts that first become payable after December 15, 2024.

Under the CRA's updated SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (June 29, 2026), depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024, qualifies as an All or Substantially All (ASA) SR&ED Capital Expenditure (claimed on line 390 of Form T661) if, at the time of acquisition, the claimant intended that the property would either: (1) be used during all or substantially all (ASA, meaning 90% or more) of its operating time in its expected useful life in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada (under subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(III) and 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(III)), or (2) have 90% or more (ASA) of its value consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Under subsection 37(1.2) and subsection 13(27) of the ITA, property becomes "available for use" at the earliest of the time it is first used by the claimant to earn income (which includes performing SR&ED) or the time it is delivered and capable of producing a commercially saleable product or service. New ASA depreciable property qualifies for both 100% inclusion in the subsection 37(1) deductible pool (replacing regular CCA on Schedule T2SCH8 pursuant to ITR paragraph 1102(1)(d)) and SR&ED ITCs (where 35% enhanced ITCs on capital property are 40% refundable). Used depreciable property qualifies for the subsection 37(1) income deduction on line 390, but is deducted as a prescribed expenditure on line 532 of Form T661 and does not earn SR&ED ITCs. Non-depreciable property (such as land, leasehold interests in land, inventory, or goodwill) and buildings or leasehold interests in buildings (except prescribed special-purpose buildings) are completely excluded from SR&ED capital expenditures.

Under the CRA's updated SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy (June 24, 2026) and subsection 127(9) of the ITA, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) provides partial ITCs for new depreciable equipment acquired after December 15, 2024, that does not meet the 90% ASA test but is actually used primarily (more than 50% and less than 90% of its operating time) for SR&ED in Canada. To qualify as SUE, the equipment must be new (not previously used or rented for any purpose), must not be general-purpose office equipment or furniture (GPOEF), and must not be Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) under ITR subsection 2900(11) (which excludes buildings, equipment for assembling/commissioning a commercial manufacturing plant under paragraph 2900(11)(c), and property intended at acquisition to be used primarily for non-SR&ED purposes under paragraph 2900(11)(d)). Unlike ASA capital property, the capital cost of SUE is not added to the subsection 37(1) deductible pool; instead, it is depreciated under standard Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) rules on Schedule T2SCH8. For ITC purposes (under both the Traditional and Proxy methods), the claimant claims 25% (1/4) of the capital cost on line 504 of Form T661 at the end of the First Period (from acquisition to the end of the first tax year ending at least 12 months after acquisition, if actual SR&ED operating time in that period exceeded 50%) and an additional 25% (1/4) of the capital cost at the end of the Second Period (from acquisition to the end of the first tax year ending at least 24 months after acquisition, if cumulative actual SR&ED operating time from acquisition exceeded 50%), up to a combined 50% of the capital cost. Any ITC claimed or refunded on SUE reduces the Undepreciated Capital Cost (UCC) of the CCA class on Schedule T2SCH8 in the following taxation year. As illustrated in Section 3.5 of the CRA's SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy, if a corporation acquires new equipment for $300,000 on January 2, 2025, and uses it 81% for SR&ED (2,900 of 3,600 operating hours) through December 31, 2026 (First Period) and 66% cumulatively (3,700 of 5,600 operating hours) through December 31, 2027 (Second Period), it claims a $75,000 qualified expenditure ($300,000 × 25%) in 2026 and another $75,000 ($300,000 × 25%) in 2027. If SUE is later sold or converted to commercial use within 20 years, subsection 127(27) recaptures the lesser of the SUE ITC earned or the ITC rate applied to 25% (if only First-Term SUE was claimed) or 50% (if both First- and Second-Term SUE were claimed) of the proceeds of disposition or FMV.

Finally, under the CRA's updated SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (June 8, 2026), equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, depend on the claimant's overhead election. Under the Traditional Method, if leased equipment is used 90% or more (ASA) of its operating time for SR&ED, 100% of the lease cost is claimable (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I)); if used less than 90% of the time, a proportional percentage matching actual SR&ED operating time can be claimed as overhead on line 360 if directly related and incremental (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) and ITR paragraph 2900(2)(c)), and leased land also qualifies as overhead under the Traditional Method. Under the Proxy Method, if leased equipment (excluding GPOEF) is used 90% or more (ASA) for SR&ED, 100% of the lease cost is claimable (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I)); if used primarily (more than 50% to less than 90%), 50% of the lease cost is claimable (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(VI)); if used 50% or less (or if for GPOEF or leased land), 0% is claimable separately. Dedicated bandwidth leased for SR&ED qualifies as an equipment lease under the Proxy Method because it utilizes dedicated optoelectronic equipment rather than GPOEF, whereas building rent is excluded under both methods (subparagraph 37(8)(d)(ii)) unless for a prescribed special-purpose building.
5. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes

Ten Canadian jurisdictions (nine provinces and Yukon) supplement the federal SR&ED programme with provincial or territorial R&D tax credits. Following the enactment of federal Bill C-15 in March 2026, provincial responses have divided into express alignment (British Columbia), major independent restructuring (Quebec), partial expansion (Saskatchewan), and retention of independent expenditure caps (Ontario, Alberta, Manitoba, and the Atlantic provinces).
5.1 Quebec: The 2025–2026 Overhaul and the New CRIC Regime

In the Quebec 2025–2026 Budget tabled on March 25, 2025, the Government of Quebec enacted a comprehensive restructuring of its provincial R&D tax incentives. Effective for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, Quebec repealed its previous suite of R&D tax credits (including the R&D salary and wage credit, the university/public research centre credit, the private partnership pre-competitive research credit, and the research consortium dues credit) and replaced them with the unified Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC / Crédit d'impôt pour la recherche, l'innovation et la commercialisation) administered by Revenu Québec.

Under official budget records and provincial tax advisory analyses, the CRIC provides a 20% base refundable tax credit across eligible expenditures above an asset-based exclusion threshold, with an enhanced 30% refundable rate reported in industry tax analyses on the first $1,000,000 of eligible expenditures above the exclusion threshold (where the asset-based exclusion threshold starts at $50,000 for small corporations). While Revenu Québec harmonizes with the federal definition of R&D (relying on the CRA's scientific review for core R&D work), the CRIC expands eligible provincial costs to cover pre-commercialisation activities performed in Quebec that are connected to R&D work carried out in Quebec by or for the corporation. Eligible pre-commercialisation work includes: (1) testing, technological validation, and studies required to obtain initial regulatory approval or certification; (2) product design involving form, aesthetics, functionality, or material selection; and (3) certain quality control activities required for initial regulatory certification. According to provincial tax advisory guides, corporate claimants file Quebec forms RD-222 and RD-1029.8.CR (replacing the legacy CO-1029.8.36 series).
5.2 Ontario: Triple-Credit Architecture (OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC)
Ontario provides three separate corporate R&D tax credits administered by the CRA:

items: Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC – Schedule T2SCH566): An 8% fully refundable tax credit for qualifying CCPCs with a permanent establishment in Ontario on up to $3.0 million of annual qualified Ontario expenditures. Ontario has not adopted the federal $6.0 million expenditure limit; its $3.0 million OITC expenditure limit phases out when the associated corporate group's prior-year federal taxable income exceeds $500,000 (eliminated at $800,000) or when prior-year specified capital reaches $25.0 million (eliminated at $50.0 million). As confirmed in the 2026 Ontario Economic Outlook and Fiscal Review, the restoration of federal SR&ED capital expenditures took effect in Ontario automatically upon the Royal Assent of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, so capital expenditures on property acquired on or after December 16, 2024, qualify for both the OITC and the ORDTC.

Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC – Schedule T2SCH508): A 3.5% non-refundable tax credit (for tax years starting after May 31, 2016; previously 4.5%) available to all corporations on eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures (reduced by any OITC claimed). Unused ORDTC credits can be carried back 3 taxation years or carried forward 20 taxation years.

Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC – Schedule T2SCH568): A 20% refundable tax credit for corporations incurring qualified expenditures under eligible R&D contracts with qualifying Ontario research institutes.
