body.text: 6. Direct Innovation Grants, Government Assistance, and Stacking Mechanics
6.1 Key Federal Direct R&D Grants and Contribution Programmes

While the SR&ED programme provides a retrospective, non-competitive tax entitlement claimed after the fiscal year-end, Canadian innovators frequently pair SR&ED with prospective, discretionary federal grants negotiated before project execution.

The most widely stacked federal grant programme for small- and medium-sized enterprises is the National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP), delivered through Industrial Technology Advisors (ITAs) to incorporated, profit-oriented Canadian SMEs with 500 or fewer employees. According to Canadian grant advisory publications (such as GrantCompass, Boast.ai, Upgraded.ai, and GovMoney), NRC IRAP provides non-repayable cost-shared grants (typically ranging from $50,000–$150,000 for early-stage firms up to $500,000–$1.0 million per project) that reimburse up to 80% of internal technical salaries and up to 50% of subcontractor costs on approved R&D projects, alongside the IRAP Youth Employment Program (providing wage subsidies for hiring recent graduates).

For large-scale industrial R&D and technology commercialisation, the federal government administers the Strategic Response Fund (originally launched in 2017 as the Strategic Innovation Fund / SIF), which received $1.0 billion over six years in Budget 2026 to catalyse large-scale innovation investments across AI, agri-food, bio-manufacturing, and clean technologies. Complementary programmes cited in industry stacking guides include Mitacs Accelerate (providing $15,000–$20,000 per internship unit for graduate students and postdoctoral fellows), NSERC Alliance Grants (funding university-industry collaborative research), and CanExport Innovation (reimbursing up to 75% of eligible costs, up to $37,500 per project and $100,000 per 12 months, for international R&D validation).
6.2 Statutory Rules for Government Assistance Reduction (ITA s. 127(9), s. 127(18) & s. 37(1)(d))

Under the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy and subsections 127(9) and 127(18) of the ITA, any government assistance (including NRC IRAP grants, concessionary government loans per CAE Inc. v. The King, provincial R&D tax credits, and provincial interactive digital media tax credits) or non-government assistance and contract payments that a claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before its income tax filing-due date for the taxation year must be deducted from both the subsection 37(1) pool (on lines 429–432 of Form T661) and the subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure pool (on lines 513–518 and 540 of Form T661) on a project-by-project basis:

Net qualified SR&ED expenditures for a project = gross qualified SR&ED expenditures for the project − (government assistance + non-government assistance + contract payments attributable to the project).
Three technical rules govern how assistance interacts with the SR&ED calculation:

items: Asymmetric Impact of Assistance on the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA): Under the Proxy Method, actual overhead is not in the subsection 37(1) deductible pool, so government assistance relating to overhead or the PPA does not reduce the subsection 37(1) pool (instead, assistance relating to the PPA or exceeding project expenditures is included in taxable income in the year received). Conversely, for ITC purposes under subsection 127(9), assistance relating to the PPA does reduce qualified SR&ED expenditures in the tax year earned.

Project-by-Project Isolation and Carryforward: Because assistance reductions apply strictly on a project-by-project basis, excess assistance on Project A does not reduce qualified expenditures on Project B in the same year; instead, unapplied excess assistance on a project is carried forward to reduce qualified SR&ED expenditures on that same project in subsequent taxation years (for example, as shown in Section 3.6.1 of the CRA's SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy, $21,000 of assistance against a $20,000 First-Period SUE expenditure reduces Year 1 qualified expenditures to $0 and carries forward the remaining $1,000 to reduce Year 2's $20,000 Second-Period SUE expenditure to $19,000).

Non-Arm's Length Assistance Allocation (Form T1145): When assistance or contract payments received by a non-arm's length party exceed that party's qualified expenditures, the unapplied excess must be allocated among non-arm's length group members performing the SR&ED using Form T1145 (Agreement to Allocate Assistance for SR&ED Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length, reported on line 540 of Form T661).

body.text: 6.3 Worked Mathematical Stacking Examples (2026 Taxation Year)

To demonstrate the exact statutory mechanics of how direct grants, the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount, and provincial R&D credits stack with the federal 35% SR&ED ITC, consider a qualifying CCPC electing the Proxy Method in its 2026 taxation year that incurs $1,000,000 in directly engaged R&D salaries in Canada (with no specified employees). Before any assistance reductions, its directly engaged salaries (Line 300) equal $1,000,000, its 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (Line 820 = 55% × $1,000,000) equals $550,000, and its gross qualified SR&ED expenditures before assistance equal $1,550,000.
Scenario A: Stacking in Ontario (OITC 8% + ORDTC 3.5% + Federal SR&ED 35%)

items: Calculate Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC at 8% on Schedule T2SCH566): 8% × $1,550,000 = $124,000 (Refundable).
Calculate Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC at 3.5% on Schedule T2SCH508, net of OITC): 3.5% × ($1,550,000 − $124,000) = 3.5% × $1,426,000 = $49,910 (Non-Refundable).
Calculate Federal SR&ED ITC (35% on Schedule T2SCH31, net of OITC and ORDTC government assistance): 35% × ($1,550,000 − $124,000 − $49,910) = 35% × $1,376,090 = $481,631.50 (Refundable).
Total Combined Tax Credits (Ontario): $124,000 + $49,910 + $481,631.50 = $655,541.50 (65.55% of the $1,000,000 cash wage expenditure).

body.text: Scenario B: Stacking in Quebec under the CRIC (30% on First $1M Above Threshold + Federal SR&ED 35%)

Applying the CRIC parameters reported in provincial R&D advisory guides (a $50,000 minimum asset-based exclusion threshold and a 30% refundable rate on the first $1,000,000 of eligible expenditures above the threshold):

items: Calculate Quebec CRIC (Form RD-1029.8.CR): 30% × ($1,000,000 − $50,000) = 30% × $950,000 = $285,000 (Refundable).
Calculate Federal SR&ED ITC (35% on Schedule T2SCH31, net of Quebec CRIC government assistance): 35% × ($1,550,000 − $285,000) = 35% × $1,265,000 = $442,750 (Refundable).
Total Combined Tax Credits (Quebec): $285,000 + $442,750 = $727,750 (72.78% of the $1,000,000 cash wage expenditure in fully refundable credits).

body.text: Scenario C: Stacking NRC IRAP Grant ($400,000) + Ontario Credits + Federal SR&ED

If the Ontario CCPC in Scenario A also receives a $400,000 NRC IRAP grant reimbursing 40% of its $1,000,000 R&D wage payroll, the 55% PPA ($550,000) is still computed on the full $1,000,000 directly engaged salary base before the $400,000 IRAP grant is deducted as government assistance from the $1,550,000 gross qualified expenditure pool:

items: Post-IRAP Qualified Expenditure Base: ($1,000,000 + $550,000) − $400,000 = $1,150,000.
Ontario OITC (8%): 8% × $1,150,000 = $92,000 (Refundable).
Ontario ORDTC (3.5%): 3.5% × ($1,150,000 − $92,000) = 3.5% × $1,058,000 = $37,030 (Non-Refundable).
Total Combined Funding (IRAP + Ontario + Federal SR&ED): $400,000 + $92,000 + $37,030 + $357,339.50 = $886,369.50 (recovering 88.64% of the $1,000,000 R&D salary expenditure).

body.text: 7. Governing Bodies, Filing Deadlines, Pre-Claim Approval, and Audit Procedures
7.1 Prescribed Forms and the Structure of Form T661

Under the CRA's SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy (updated January 28, 2025), a claimant must submit its income tax return (Form T2 for corporations, Form T1 for individuals, or Form T3 for trusts) together with Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim) and either Schedule T2SCH31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations) or Form T2038(IND) (Investment Tax Credit (Individuals)) containing all "prescribed information" by its SR&ED reporting deadline.
Form T661 is organized into ten parts:

items: Part 1 (General Information): Claimant name (line 010), 15-character Business Number, tax year dates, total number of projects claimed (line 050), and contact details (lines 100–125).

Part 2 (Project Information – Sections A to C): Technical project descriptions prepared by personnel familiar with the scientific or technological content, detailing the project completion date, scientific or technological uncertainties, chronological description of hypotheses formulated, experiments/analyses conducted, results obtained, and logical conclusions (line 244), internal or external preparer disclosures (lines 253–259), up to three key directly involved individuals and their qualifications (lines 260–261), foreign SR&ED wage indicators (line 265), work performed on behalf of others (line 266), and contractor disclosures (lines 267–269). Claimants with more than 20 projects may elect to file Part 2 with their return for only the 20 largest projects in dollar value, provided they complete and maintain Part 2 descriptions for all claimed projects at their place of business for immediate submission upon CRA request, and include the costs of every project in Part 6.

Part 3 (Calculation of SR&ED Expenditures – Sections A to C): Reporting allowable current and capital expenditures (lines 300–400) and computing the subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures.

Part 4 (Calculation of Qualified SR&ED Expenditures for ITC Purposes): Computing the subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure pool, including the PPA, Shared-Use Equipment (line 504), Form T1146 transfers in/out (lines 510 and 546), provincial/federal/non-government assistance (lines 514, 516, 517, 518, and Form T1145 allocations on line 540), unpaid current expenditures (line 520), non-taxable supplier exclusions (line 528), the 20% reduction on arm's-length contracts and third-party payments (line 529), prescribed expenditures (lines 530 and 532), non-taxable income deductions (line 535), and NAL supplier adjustments (lines 542 and 543).

Part 5 (Calculation of Prescribed Proxy Amount – Sections A and B): Computing the salary base (lines 810–814), specified employee caps (lines 850–858), and the 55% PPA (line 820) when the Proxy Method is elected.
Part 6 (Project Costs): Mandatory project-by-project expenditure breakdown for every project claimed in the taxation year.
Part 7 (Additional Information) and Part 8 (Claim Checklist).
Part 9 (Claim Preparer Information): Mandatory disclosures for every claim preparer that accepted consideration to prepare or assist in preparing the claim.
Part 10 (Certification): Signature of an authorized signing officer.

body.text: 7.2 The Absolute 18-Month Statutory Filing Deadline (ITA s. 37(11), s. 127(9)(m) & s. 220(2.2))

Under subsection 37(11), subsection 37(11.1), and paragraph 127(9)(m) of the Income Tax Act, a claimant's SR&ED reporting deadline is strictly 12 months after the filing-due date of the claimant's income tax return for the taxation year in which the expenditure was incurred. Because a corporation's T2 income tax return is due 6 months after the end of its taxation year, a corporation's overall SR&ED reporting deadline is 18 months after the end of its taxation year. If a corporation's tax year ends on the last day of a month (e.g., February 28, 2024), its T2 due date is the last day of the 6th month (August 31, 2024) and its SR&ED reporting deadline is the last day of the 18th month (August 31, 2025); if its tax year ends on a specific numerical day (e.g., January 6, 2024), its T2 due date is July 6, 2024, and its SR&ED reporting deadline is July 6, 2025.

Crucially, under subsection 220(2.2) of the Income Tax Act, the Minister of National Revenue and the CRA are statutorily barred by law from granting any extension of time to file prescribed SR&ED forms or prescribed information past the 18-month reporting deadline. Any expenditure or project not reported on prescribed forms on or before the 18-month deadline is permanently disallowed. If a claimant files its claim at least 90 days before the 18-month reporting deadline, the CRA has sufficient time to perform an initial completeness review and notify the claimant of any missing information so that the deficiency can be cured before the 18-month deadline expires. (Two exceptions apply: deducting amounts in a subsequent year from a subsection 37(1) pool whose expenditures were timely reported within 18 months is not subject to the 18-month deadline, and Part 9 claim preparer disclosures are exempt from the 18-month deadline).
7.3 The New CRA Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 1, 2026) and Review Service Standards

On April 1, 2026, the CRA launched its new optional Pre-Claim Approval process (building upon earlier Pre-Claim Consultation / Pre-Claim Review pilots and complementing the mandatory First-Time Claimant Advisory Service [FTCAS] for first-time claimants or businesses that have not claimed SR&ED in the preceding 3 years). Submitted through the SR&ED Client Portal inside My Business Account, the Pre-Claim Approval process allows eligible businesses to obtain a formal upfront determination from the CRA on whether their proposed R&D projects qualify for SR&ED tax incentives within 8 weeks—before starting the R&D work or incurring costs.

In conjunction with automated Preliminary Risk Assessment screening in the CRA's CORTAX/AIMS mainframe system (where approximately 80% of SR&ED claims are filed electronically and roughly 40% of claims are accepted as filed without manual audit, reinforced by AI-supported claim screening introduced in 2025), the CRA enforces three processing service standards for refundable SR&ED claims (counted from receipt of a complete claim and tax return; no service standards apply to non-refundable claims):

items: Within 60 Days: Refundable claims that are accepted as filed.
Within 90 Days: Refundable claims selected for review that only include projects that were granted Pre-Claim Approval.
Within 180 Days: Refundable claims selected for review that include any project that was not granted Pre-Claim Approval or that materially differs from what was previously granted Pre-Claim Approval.

body.text: 7.4 Coordinated RTA/FR Audits, Statutory Penalties, and Dispute Resolution

When a claim is selected for review, a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) (trained under the CRA Claim Review Manual curriculum covering eligibility, report writing, documentation, risk-based review, and business context) and a Financial Reviewer (FR) conduct a coordinated review. The RTA and FR coordinate their information requests and on-site or virtual interviews with senior technical and financial personnel, cross-check joint technical-financial issues (such as employee time allocations, shareholder status of specified employees, and experimental vs. commercial production runs), and share the draft SR&ED Review Report and Proposal Letter before issuing it to the claimant.
Two specific statutory penalties govern non-compliant SR&ED filings:

items: Part 9 Claim Preparer Penalty ($1,000): If the prescribed information in Part 9 of Form T661 regarding claim preparers and their billing arrangements is missing, incomplete, or inaccurate, a $1,000 penalty may be assessed for which the claimant and the claim preparer are jointly and severally (or solidarily) liable. Missing or inaccurate Part 9 information does not result in the disallowance of the SR&ED claim itself.

Gross Negligence Penalty for Overstated SR&ED Claims (Subsection 163(2) of the ITA): Under the CRA's Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims Policy (updated January 28, 2025) and subsections 163(2), 163(2.1), and 163(3) (specifically paragraphs 163(2)(a) and 163(2)(d)) of the ITA, if a claimant knowingly, or under circumstances amounting to gross negligence, makes or participates in a false statement or omission in an initial or amended return (such as claiming fabricated projects that never occurred, disguising personal expenses or false invoices as SR&ED, or continuing to claim ineligible, miscalculated, or unsubstantiated amounts after receiving prior written advice from the CRA where those amounts are not under objection or appeal), the CRA may assess a penalty equal to the greater of $100 or 50% of the understated Part I tax plus the overstated refundable ITC claimed: Penalty = greater of $100 and 50% × (understated Part I tax + overstated refundable ITC claimed). Under subsection 163(3), the CRA bears the burden of proving on a balance of probabilities that the false statement resulted from knowing misconduct or gross negligence rather than simple oversight or misunderstanding. Disallowed SR&ED expenses that are legitimate business expenses do not understate income for Part I tax purposes, whereas non-business expenses (such as personal expenses or false invoices) overstate the subsection 37(1) pool (which the CRA deems to be deducted first, computing theoretical Part I tax under subsection 163(2.1) even if the claimant is in a net loss position). However, when the gross negligence penalty applies to an overstated refundable ITC under paragraph 163(2)(d), the 50% penalty is calculated on the entire overstated refund claimed.

body.text: If a claimant disagrees with a review outcome, it may first discuss the issue with the RTA and/or FR, escalate unresolved concerns to the Research and Technology Manager (RTM) and/or Financial Review Manager (FRM) (or request a formal Administrative Review regarding review conduct), file a formal Notice of Objection within 90 days from the date of the Notice of Assessment or Reassessment, and subsequently appeal an adverse objection decision to the Tax Court of Canada and the Federal Court of Appeal.
8. Landmark Canadian Case Law and Judicial Precedents
8.1 Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520 (TCC)

Decided on May 1, 1998, by Justice Donald G.H. Bowman of the Tax Court of Canada, Northwest Hydraulic is the foundational judicial precedent governing SR&ED eligibility in Canada. At paragraph 16, Justice Bowman established the five criteria used to determine whether an activity constitutes SR&ED:

items: Technological Risk or Uncertainty: Was there a technological risk or uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures (defined as techniques, procedures, and data generally accessible to competent professionals in the field)?

Formulation of Hypotheses: Did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty through a five-stage process culminating in the formulation of hypotheses and their methodical testing?

Accordance with the Scientific Method: Did the procedures adopted accord with the total discipline of the scientific method, characterized by trained and systematic observation, measurement, and experiment, and the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses?

Technological Advancement: Did the process result in a technological advancement (an advancement in the general understanding)? Justice Bowman emphasized that the fact that the initial objective is not achieved invalidates neither the hypothesis formed nor the methods used; on the contrary, failure can reinforce the measure of the technological uncertainty.
Contemporaneous Detailed Records: Did the taxpayer keep a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and the results as the work progressed?

body.text: 8.2 RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, 99 DTC 5087, 235 N.R. 258 (FCA) & C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393, 2002 DTC 6740 (FCA)

In RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen (decided December 21, 1998, at paragraph 10), the Federal Court of Appeal formally endorsed Justice Bowman's five-part Northwest Hydraulic approach as binding appellate law. Three years later, in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada (decided December 11, 2001, per Sexton J.A., Docket A-601-00), the Federal Court of Appeal unanimously dismissed an appeal from Judge Bonner's Tax Court decision disallowing 1991–1995 SR&ED claims by a global lottery ticket telemarketer that developed a multilingual computer and telephone system handling 2 to 3 million customers and up to 25,000 daily purchases. Reaffirming Northwest Hydraulic and RIS-Christie at paragraph 17, the FCA upheld Judge Bonner's conclusion that the software development did not constitute SR&ED and noted Judge Bonner's observation that the taxpayer's stated software objective was not a "hypothesis capable of being proved or disproved by means of scientific research".
8.3 Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen, 2011 FCA 355, Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. The Queen, 2021 FCA 88, & National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72

In Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen (2011 TCC 261, aff'd 2011 FCA 355 on December 15, 2011), the Tax Court and Federal Court of Appeal rejected an SR&ED claim for redesigning "Multi-Bins" thermoformed plastic storage bins to be smaller and lighter, holding that using a heat sink during thermoforming was routine engineering and that the SR&ED program was never intended to subsidize routine product development.

In Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Her Majesty the Queen (2019 TCC 246 per Owen J., aff'd 2021 FCA 88 on May 10, 2021, per Webb J.A., concurred in by Near and Boivin JJ.A., Docket A-442-19), the taxpayer appealed the denial of its 2009 and 2010 SR&ED claims. Kam-Press conceded that if Northwest Hydraulic was good law, the Tax Court's finding at paragraph 29 that it failed to follow the scientific method was fatal to its appeal, but argued that because the definition of SR&ED had been moved from the Income Tax Regulations to ITA subsection 248(1) and the exact phrase "scientific method" does not appear in the statute, Criterion #3 of Northwest Hydraulic should not apply. Citing Canada Trustco Mortgage Co. v. Canada (2005 SCC 54 at para. 10) on textual, contextual, and purposive statutory interpretation, Justice Webb noted that Justice Bowman was interpreting the statutory definition of SR&ED and pointed to a continuous line of binding FCA decisions—RIS-Christie (1998), C.W. Agencies (2001), Jentel Manufacturing (2011), and R&D Pro-Innovation Inc. v. Canada (2016 FCA 152)—that endorsed Northwest Hydraulic. The FCA dismissed Kam-Press's appeal with costs. The Federal Court of Appeal and Tax Court maintained this same strict alignment between the statutory definition in subsection 248(1) and the Northwest Hydraulic criteria in National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72 (affirming 2020 TCC 66) and Canafric Inc. v. The King, 2023 TCC 105 (July 26, 2023).
8.4 Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 6

Decided on January 17, 2017, by Justice Don R. Sommerfeldt of the Tax Court of Canada (Docket 2015-125(IT)I), Joel Theatrical Rigging disallowed 2008 and 2009 SR&ED claims for two stage-rigging projects: the "Fire Curtain Project" (developing a counterweight-free hydraulic system to lower a theatre fire curtain within 30 seconds by hoisting an 800-pound weight in the shop and watching it fall while manually reapplying a brake and adding hydraulic pumps/valves) and the "Manual Override Project" (replacing retaining bolts with a hand-crank system so a cable drum could disengage during power outages without losing limit-switch calibration). Justice Sommerfeldt dismissed both claims on four grounds:

items: No Technological Uncertainty Proven: Neither the company president (who had a Grade 12 education and 36 years of rigging experience) nor its tax preparer was a professional engineer or scientist, and the company failed to prove that the problems could not have been solved by routine engineering had they consulted a professional engineer.

Failure to Follow the Scientific Method: Testing lacked systematic observation and quantitative measurement; employees watched falling weights with the naked eye without using a stopwatch, measuring velocity/acceleration, or conducting controlled hypothesis testing.
No Technological Advancement: The projects achieved practical mechanical functionality but did not advance general mechanical engineering knowledge.
Insufficient Contemporaneous Records: Detailed records of hypotheses, tests, and quantitative results were not maintained as the work progressed.

body.text: 8.5 CAE Inc. v. His Majesty the King, 2022 FCA 178 (aff'g 2021 TCC 57; SCC Leave Refused May 26, 2023) & Immunovaccine Technologies Inc. v. Canada, 2014 FCA 196

Decided on October 19, 2022, by the Federal Court of Appeal (per Boivin J.A., Docket A-264-21), CAE Inc. addressed whether $250 million in contributions ($57 million in 2012 and $59 million in 2013) received by CAE Inc. from Industry Canada under the Strategic Aerospace and Defence Initiative (SADI) constituted "government assistance" under subsection 127(9) and paragraph 12(1)(x) of the Income Tax Act. Although the SADI agreement was an unconditionally repayable loan requiring CAE to repay 135% of the advances ($337.5 million, yielding an annual return of approximately 2.5%) over 15 years, it included policy covenants requiring exclusive manufacturing in Canada, university R&D collaboration, and IP restrictions. Applying Canada v. Consumers' Gas Co. ([1987] 2 F.C. 60), Canada v. CCLC Technologies Inc. ([1996] F.C.J. No. 1226), and Immunovaccine Technologies Inc. v. Canada (2014 FCA 196), the Tax Court and Federal Court of Appeal held that because the loan terms were concessionary and not strictly commercial, the SADI advances constituted "government assistance" that both reduced CAE's SR&ED ITCs and had to be included in taxable income. The Supreme Court of Canada denied leave to appeal on May 26, 2023.
8.6 Summary Table of Leading Canadian SR&ED Jurisprudence

body.text: 9. Audit Readiness and Strategic Compliance Checklist for Canadian Claimants

To ensure full statutory compliance and withstand a coordinated CRA Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) and Financial Reviewer (FR) review under the post-Bill C-15 regime, Canadian claimants should execute the following five verification steps:

items: Model the CCPC / ECPC Phase-Out Election (ITA s. 127(10.32)): For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, compare the associated corporate group's prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada against its 3-year consolidated average annual gross revenue across the $15.0 million to $75.0 million phase-out range, and file the subsection 127(10.32) election if the revenue method preserves a higher share of the $6.0 million enhanced 35% expenditure limit.

Segregate New vs. Used Capital Property and Log SUE Operating Hours: Confirm that all capital equipment claimed on Form T661 was acquired and became available for use after December 15, 2024. Ensure used depreciable property is claimed only in the subsection 37(1) deductible pool (line 390) and excluded as a prescribed expenditure from the ITC calculation on line 532. For new equipment used between 50% and 90% of its operating time for SR&ED, maintain contemporaneous operating-hour logs from the date of availability for use to substantiate the 25% First-Term (at 12 months or more) and 25% Second-Term (at 24 months or more) Shared-Use Equipment ITC claims on line 504.

Utilize the April 1, 2026 CRA Pre-Claim Approval Portal: Before commencing major R&D projects, submit an optional Pre-Claim Approval application via My Business Account to obtain a formal eligibility determination from the CRA within 8 weeks and qualify for the accelerated 90-day review service standard on refundable claims.

Enforce the 180-Day Payment Cutoff After Fiscal Year-End: Verify that all accrued SR&ED salaries, non-specified employee bonuses, arm's-length contractor invoices, and non-arm's length Form T1146 amounts are paid on or before the 180th day following the end of the taxation year to prevent current-year disallowance on lines 315 and 520 of Form T661.

Maintain Contemporaneous Technical and Financial Records for 6 to 20 Years: Structure engineering logs, test records, and project documentation around the CRA's "Why" and "How" Requirements, recording the specific technological uncertainties, hypotheses formulated, quantitative experimental measurements (avoiding the naked-eye observation flaw of Joel Theatrical Rigging, 2017 TCC 6), and logical conclusions. Retain all supporting books and records for a minimum of 6 years from the end of the taxation year to which they relate under paragraph 230(4)(b) of the Income Tax Act, and retain acquisition and usage records for capital property, SUE, and transformed materials for the full 20-year ITC recapture window under subsections 127(27) and 127(36).
